sections.title: Executive investment summary: a state-owned monopoly asset trading on a private-market multiple

blocks.text: Mazagon Dock Shipbuilders Ltd (MDL) is a Navratna defence public sector undertaking under the administrative control of the Ministry of Defence that builds, repairs and refits warships, conventional submarines and offshore structures from a single waterfront complex in Mumbai plus a yard at Nhava. [F] (AR2026 p.131) It is described as the only Indian shipyard to have built both destroyers and conventional submarines for the Indian Navy, and the only one with two independent submarine assembly and launch lines. [F] (AR2026 p.32) (AR2026 p.42)

Revenue is recognised on the percentage-of-completion (input/cost) basis across multi-year contracts, so reported sales are an accounting measure of production progress rather than of cash billings. [F] (AR2026 p.152) Management confirmed profit is recognised from the beginning of a project on estimated cost-to-complete, with no minimum completion threshold. [MC] (CALL Nov 2024)

Revenue from the Ministry of Defence was Rs 11,077 cr in FY26 against standalone revenue of Rs 12,840 cr, i.e. **86% of revenue from a single counterparty** [E] (AR2026 p.223) (AR2026 p.208); in FY25 the same ratio was 90% [E]. Listing status: MDL listed on BSE and NSE in 2020 [F] (AR2026 p.31), so there is a five-year listed disclosure record. The evidence base is nevertheless thinner than the listing date suggests: the company is exempted from Ind AS 108 segment reporting as a producer of defence equipment [F] (AR2026 p.211), it takes the Ind AS 24 government-entity exemption on related-party detail [F] (AR2026 p.222), it discloses no capacity or utilisation data, and no earnings call transcript is available for either Q4 FY26 or Q1 FY27 - the most recent transcript in our evidence set is the Q2 FY26 call of 28 October 2025.

subsections.title: Bear thesis: the strongest reasons not to own it

items: 1. The order book has more than halved in four years and fell again in the latest quarter. Disclosed order book: Rs 45,874 cr (FY22), Rs 38,755 cr (FY23), Rs 38,561 cr (FY24), Rs 32,260 cr (FY25), Rs 20,535 cr (FY26) [F] (AR2026 p.36), and Rs 18,218 cr at 30 June 2026 [F] (PPT Jul 2026). That is roughly 1.37x trailing revenue [E] (NUMBERS) (PPT Jul 2026) - thin for a business with 6-9 year build cycles.

2. The two contracts the entire growth narrative rests on are still unsigned. The three additional P75 Scorpene submarines were 'confident... before 31st March' in February 2025 [MC] (CALL Feb 2025), 'maybe as early as next month' in May 2025 [MC] (CALL Jun 2025), and by October 2025 had gone to 'we haven't received an update' [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). P75I was expected to be signed 'by this financial year' in October 2025 [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). Neither appears in the 30 June 2026 order book [F] (PPT Jul 2026), and no award announcement appears in the exchange filings through 8 September 2026 [F] (ANNOUNCEMENTS).

3. Cash conversion has broken down. Consolidated CFO was minus Rs 2,654 cr in FY26 against reported PAT of Rs 2,578 cr; cumulative CFO over three years is 0.02x cumulative PAT and three-year free cash flow is minus Rs 1,183 cr [F] (NUMBERS). The mechanism is visible: gross customer advances fell from Rs 23,803 cr to Rs 18,427 cr [F] (AR2026 p.208) and contract liabilities fell from Rs 15,494 cr to Rs 10,303 cr [F] (AR2026 p.167).

4. Reported profit leans heavily on non-operating income and on provision reversals. Other income was Rs 1,139 cr, 35% of PBT [F] (NUMBERS), of which Rs 1,025 cr was bank deposit interest [F] (AR2026 p.209). Separately FY26 revenue absorbed a Rs 262 cr reversal of excess P17A liquidated damages [F] (AR2026 p.231) and the P&L benefited from a Rs 90 cr write-back of inventory provisions [F] (AR2026 p.232) and a Rs 81 cr write-back of guarantee-repair provisions [F] (AR2026 p.211).

5. Fixed-price contracts are already loss-making at the margin. The auditor flagged as a key audit matter a provision for expected loss on onerous contracts of Rs 1,060 cr at 31 March 2026 (PY Rs 521 cr) [F] (AR2026 p.153); total estimated loss on those contracts is Rs 1,180 cr [F] (AR2026 p.231). Management attributed this to component price inflation after the 2022-23 bids on the Coast Guard FPV and the Denmark MPV contracts [MC] (CALL Jun 2025).

6. Single-customer, single-location, single-shareholder concentration. 86% of FY26 revenue came from the MoD [E] (AR2026 p.223); production is concentrated on the Mumbai waterfront plus Nhava [F] (AR2026 p.42); the President of India holds 81.22% [F] (AR2026 p.117). Management itself puts 80-90% of the order book with the Indian Navy [MC] (CALL Nov 2025).

7. Management's own normalised margin guidance is far below reported margins. Successive CFOs and CMDs have guided to 12-15% PBT margin as normal for the industry [MC] (CALL Nov 2024) (CALL Feb 2025) and 'approximately 15%' EBITDA-equivalent for new projects [MC] (CALL Nov 2025), against FY26 reported PBT/revenue of 25% [F] (AR2026 p.39). The gap is explained as end-of-project true-ups that do not repeat [MC] (CALL Nov 2025).

8. Revenue quality is deteriorating on the balance sheet. Unbilled trade receivables jumped from Rs 145 cr to Rs 1,577 cr in one year [F] (AR2026 p.201); debtor days rose from 34 to 73 [F] (NUMBERS); and the auditor's emphasis of matter records that balances due to/from the Indian Navy remain subject to reconciliation and confirmation [F] (AR2026 p.151) (AR2026 p.213).

9. The valuation demands growth that no disclosed evidence supports. The reverse DCF implies about 56% compound sales growth for five years to justify today's enterprise value, against 14.2% in the base case [F] (NUMBERS). Every scenario in our DCF - bear, base and bull - sits far below the current price [F] (NUMBERS).

10. Governance frictions typical of a CPSE. The secretarial auditor reported that the Board's composition was not compliant with the Companies Act and SEBI LODR independent-director and independent woman-director requirements during parts of FY26, and that vacancies were not filled within the timelines under Regulation 17(1E) [F] (AR2026 p.92). Four independent directors and the government nominee turned over inside about fourteen months [F] (AR2026 p.102).

blocks.text: Our variant view is that MDL is simultaneously a better business and a worse security than the market treats it as. The asset - two independent submarine lines, a 250-year waterfront, a trained integration workforce and state-conferred qualification - is close to irreplaceable, and the FY21-FY26 margin transformation was real, not cosmetic. But the equity is not priced as a Rs 13,000 cr revenue engineering company with a shrinking backlog, deteriorating cash conversion and a customer that sets its prices; it is priced as though the P75-AS, P75I, P17B and LPD programmes are already won. The disclosed order book at 30 June 2026 is Rs 18,218 cr [F] (PPT Jul 2026), of which roughly Rs 9,548 cr sits on programmes where every vessel has already been delivered and only spares, guarantee and residual obligations remain [E] (PPT Jul 2026). Our reverse DCF says the price requires about 56% annual sales growth for five years [F] (NUMBERS). The gap between those two numbers, not the quality of the yard, is the investment question.

subsections.title: What the timeline reveals about how recent this business really is

blocks.text: The institution is 250 years old; the financial profile that supports today's valuation is five years old. Sales were Rs 4,048 cr in FY21 and Rs 13,006 cr in FY26, and operating margin went from 6% to 17% over the same span [F] (NUMBERS). Every element of that transformation traces to two contracts signed in 2011 and 2015 - P15B destroyers and P17A frigates - reaching their delivery phase between FY22 and FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.68). Both are now fully delivered [F] (PPT Jul 2026).

The corollary is uncomfortable and is the core of the bear case: the company has not yet demonstrated a full contract cycle at the current scale on contracts it won recently. The recently won book - Coast Guard vessels (Rs 2,991 cr, signed Oct 2023 to Jan 2024) [F] (AR2026 p.71), the Denmark MPVs (USD 85 mn / Rs 715 cr) [F] (AR2026 p.71) and ONGC offshore - is precisely the portion carrying a Rs 1,060 cr onerous-contract provision and turnkey-outsourced subcontracting economics [F] (AR2026 p.153) (MC) (CALL Nov 2025). sections.title: Business model: where value is captured in a nomination-led, fixed-price build chain

subsections.title: The production chain, step by step

items: 1. Qualification. Naval shipbuilding eligibility is a state process: for P75I, MDL's technical offer was accepted and only its bid was found technically suitable, after which price bids were opened [MC] (CALL Feb 2025). For the three additional Scorpenes, MDL says it is nominated rather than bidding [MC] (CALL Nov 2024).

2. Pre-contract design and tendering, at MDL's cost. The company charged Rs 100.60 cr to the P&L in FY26 (FY25: Rs 35.72 cr) on concept and design work for a future contract that has not been awarded, with no revenue recognised [F] (AR2026 p.231). 'Pre-contract expenses' in other expenses were Rs 99.46 cr against Rs 36.80 cr [F] (AR2026 p.210). Management confirms that if contract signature is delayed, MDL receives no compensation [MC] (CALL Jun 2025).

3. Contracting, almost entirely fixed-price. Management states that of the then Rs 32,260 cr order book about Rs 20,000 cr was fixed-price with reasonably high margins and the rest fixed-price at lower margins; ONGC contracts are partly cost-plus with one fixed-price PRP contract [MC] (CALL Jun 2025) (CALL Nov 2025).

4. Design freeze and procurement. Raw material and equipment costs are negotiated and effectively locked at the early stage of the project, with staggered delivery to control inventory [MC] (CALL Jun 2025). Imports were 15.31% of revenue in FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.142).

5. Fabrication, block assembly and integration. Three dry docks, three wet basins, three large slipways, six small slipways, a 300-tonne Goliath crane and a retractable-roof module workshop on the shipbuilding side; a dedicated submarine dry dock, shore integration facility and cradle assembly shop on the submarine side [F] (AR2026 p.42).

6. Subcontracting and outsourcing. Management distinguishes subcontracting (third-party labour inside MDL premises) from outsourcing (work performed off-site, with transport cost), and says executing outside is costlier; with about 27 ships running concurrently the asking rate forces outsourcing [MC] (CALL Jun 2025). Offshore project execution is described as 'virtually turnkey outsourcing' [MC] (CALL Nov 2025).

7. Revenue recognition. Percentage of completion, measured on inputs (cost incurred), with penalties deducted from revenue [F] (AR2026 p.152). Contract revenue recognised in FY26 was Rs 12,809 cr [F] (AR2026 p.152).

8. Delivery, D448 acceptance, guarantee period and base-and-depot spares. Revenue is not exhausted at delivery: warranty obligations, a mandatory dry-docking inspection during the guarantee period, and spares supply follow [MC] (CALL Nov 2024). Guarantee repairs are normally held at about 10% of ship cost [MC] (CALL Nov 2025); base and depot spares at about 15% of project cost [MC] (CALL Jun 2025).

9. Cost true-up. If the guarantee-period and D448 liabilities cost less than provided, the difference releases to profit - the mechanism management repeatedly cites for the FY24-FY26 margin level [MC] (CALL Nov 2024) (CALL Jun 2025).

subsections.title: Where value is captured, and why

blocks.text: Value is captured at two points and almost nowhere else. First, at integration and project management on repeat platforms, where accumulated learning lets MDL complete below bid cost - management is explicit that FY24-FY26 margins came from 'projects at a late stage where greater revenue recognition and profitability were accrued and these projects were actually also obtained at significantly good margins' [MC] (CALL Jun 2025). Second, at the tail of a programme, when guarantee and D448 provisions are released [MC] (CALL Nov 2024).

Value is not captured on price. These are fixed-price contracts on which raw-material cost is locked early [MC] (CALL Jun 2025), the counterparty is the customer that also sets the procurement rules, and management observes that efficiency gains 'would be taken into consideration definitely by the customer also when we negotiate for future projects' [MC] (CALL Nov 2024). That is a clear statement that productivity gains are recycled into the next contract price rather than retained. [AI] The FY26 onerous-contract provision of Rs 1,060 cr [F] (AR2026 p.153) is the same mechanism running in reverse when input costs rise after the bid.

Outsourcing and capital intensity: capex has averaged 1.3-7.0% of sales over the last three years (FY24 3.6%, FY25 7.0%, FY26 1.3%) [F] (NUMBERS), and fixed-asset turnover was 6.3x in FY26 [F] (NUMBERS). Gross block was Rs 2,140 cr against Rs 12,840 cr of standalone revenue [F] (AR2026 p.36) (AR2026 p.39). On the asset base alone MDL looks asset-light; on the working-capital base it is anything but - total assets of Rs 27,474 cr support Rs 13,006 cr of sales, with the difference sitting in customer-advance-funded inventory and cash [E] (NUMBERS). The honest classification is **working-capital-heavy and fixed-asset-light, financed by the customer** [AI].

subsections.title: Deep dive 1 - Conventional submarines: the whole thesis in one programme

blocks.text: Where MDL sits in the value chain: MDL is the licensed builder and integrator, not the designer. Scorpene P75 was built under licence in collaboration with Naval Group of France [F] (AR2026 p.68); P75I would be built with TKMS technology transfer, with management claiming more than 60% indigenous content, higher than Scorpene [MC] (CALL Jun 2025). The design IP sits abroad; the assembly, integration, testing and lifecycle support sit at MDL.

What exists today versus narrative. Exists: six Scorpene submarines delivered, the last (INS Vagsheer) commissioned January 2025, with D448 second-reading acceptance for INS Vagir signed 22 April 2026 [F] (AR2026 p.68) (PPT Jul 2026). Exists: a claimed capacity to build eleven submarines simultaneously, up from six, after commissioning a submarine section assembly workshop [MC] (CALL Jun 2025); two independent submarine assembly and launch lines [F] (AR2026 p.42); an extension to the submarine launch facility at Kasara Basin and East Yard infrastructure for pressure-hull fabrication in progress [F] (AR2026 p.42) (AR2026 p.72). Exists: an AIP plug contract of Rs 1,768 cr received December 2024, of which Rs 1,542 cr remains [MC] (CALL Feb 2025) [F] (PPT Jul 2026), and an MRLC refit contract of Rs 2,421 cr with Rs 492 cr remaining [F] (PPT Jul 2026). Narrative only: three additional Scorpenes, six P75I boats, exports to unnamed third countries, and TKMS routing global orders through MDL. [AI]

Anchor-customer exposure, quantified: 100% of the submarine business is MoD. Balance submarine-related order book is Rs 3,712 cr (P75 residual Rs 1,678 cr, MRLC Rs 492 cr, AIP Rs 1,542 cr), 20.4% of total backlog [E] (PPT Jul 2026). Against a claimed capacity for eleven concurrent submarines, there is currently no submarine under construction - only residual work, one refit and one AIP integration. [AI]

So FY26's 17% margin is not flattered on a net basis by these items; the concern is different and more serious - **the gross amount of profit passing through provision accounts each year now exceeds Rs 1,000 cr, on a reported EBITDA of Rs 2,268 cr.** [E] (AR2026 p.211) Earnings are heavily estimate-dependent in both directions.

Part of the improvement is structural and should be respected: the value-added ratio moved from 0.28-0.30 (FY22-FY24) to 0.35-0.39 (FY25-FY26) [F] (AR2026 p.39), employee cost fell from 7.77% to 6.70% of income [F] (AR2026 p.65), and MDL delivered eight major combatants on or ahead of schedule, which on management's account earns the yard money [MC] (CALL Jun 2025). Those are real.

But management has been unusually consistent in saying the level is not sustainable. Two successive finance directors have guided to 12-15% PBT margin as normal for the industry [MC] (CALL Nov 2024) (CALL Feb 2025); the CMD said in May 2025 'it is safe to have a guidance of approximately 15%' and 'we cannot keep this as a standard profit margin that a shipyard can get' [MC] (CALL Jun 2025); and in October 2025 the finance director said explicitly that the 25-30% margins visible in the accounts arise 'only when we are at the completion of the project and we book all the unclaimed liabilities', whereas new projects would be 'around 12% to 15%' [MC] (CALL Nov 2025). Reported PBT to revenue was 25% in FY26 [F] (AR2026 p.39).

Our conclusion: **the margin improvement is about half structural and half cycle-position.** The structural half - learning-curve efficiency, better project management, a higher value-added ratio - is worth perhaps 4-6 points versus FY22. The cycle half came from completing two mega-programmes simultaneously, and it is running out: the entire large-combatant backlog has been delivered, the replacement book is loss-provided, and management's own normalised guidance is 12-15%. blocks.text: Three caveats govern everything below. First, the basis shifts: FY17-FY25 in our statements data is effectively standalone (MDL had no subsidiary), while FY26 consolidates Colombo Dockyard from 19 January 2026 and a 47.21% associate's profit share; year-on-year comparisons are therefore not fully like-for-like. Second, the company is exempt from segment reporting [F] (AR2026 p.211), so no profitability can be attributed to any product line. Third, our statements data's quarterly profit columns do not sum to its annual profit columns (see the discrepancy table below), so quarterly and annual analyses must be kept apart.

sections.title: Working capital: the number that decides whether this business generates cash

blocks.text: Two working-capital measures are available for the same date and they point in opposite directions. Our statements data shows working capital days of minus 187 - negative working capital, i.e. the customer funds the business [F] (NUMBERS). The annual report's ten-year table shows working capital of **positive** Rs 6,453.89 cr at 31 March 2026, up from Rs 4,890.78 cr [F] (AR2026 p.39), because it defines working capital as current assets less current liabilities and those current assets include Rs 12,878 cr of cash and bank balances held against customer advances [E] (AR2026 p.167).

Neither number describes the operating reality on its own. The real question for a shipyard on percentage-of-completion is simpler: **is the customer ahead of MDL or is MDL ahead of the customer?** In FY25 the customer was far ahead (gross advances Rs 23,803 cr). In FY26 that gap closed by Rs 5,375 cr [F] (AR2026 p.208), and simultaneously MDL's unbilled receivables rose Rs 1,432 cr [F] (AR2026 p.201). Both movements go the same way: MDL is progressively financing more of the work itself. [AI]

blocks.text: The cash conversion cycle looks superb - minus 20 days - and it is meaningless in isolation. It is negative only because inventory has been consumed into delivered ships while payables remain outstanding. **The metric that matters is working capital days moving from -426 to -187 in two years** [F] (NUMBERS): the customer-funded cushion that has historically financed this business is shrinking by roughly 120 days a year, and nothing in the current order book obviously refills it. A new mega-contract would refill it with a fresh advance; that is a further reason why contract signature, not margin, is the key variable. [AI]

blocks.text: MDL competes in three quite different arenas and its position is different in each. In conventional submarines it is close to a monopoly - the only Indian yard to have built them, with two independent assembly lines, nominated rather than bid for the P75 follow-on and the only technically suitable P75I bidder [F] (AR2026 p.32) (AR2026 p.42) [MC] (CALL Nov 2024) (CALL Feb 2025). In large surface combatants it is a strong but contestable incumbent; the loss of the next-generation corvette to GRSE and GSL, and the need to team with Swan Defence to bid a 200-metre landing platform dock, both demonstrate the limits [MC] (CALL Jun 2025) (CALL Nov 2025). In small patrol vessels, commercial ships, offshore EPC and ship repair it is a price-taker competing with private yards, and the Rs 1,060 cr onerous-contract provision is the measured cost of that position [F] (AR2026 p.153).

The defining structural feature of this industry is that **the customer owns most of the competitors.** The Ministry of Defence owns MDL, GRSE, GSL and HSL and allocates work among them; MDL itself holds 47.21% of one of its competitors [F] (AR2026 p.99) [MC] (CALL Jun 2025). No non-compete or conflict-management disclosure addresses this anywhere in the annual report. For a minority shareholder, competitive outcomes are therefore an administrative allocation, not a market result. [AI]

subsections.title: The two questions the scores cannot answer

items: **Does the moat produce pricing power or only order security?** Every piece of evidence points to the latter. Management states that efficiency gains will be 'taken into consideration definitely by the customer also when we negotiate for future projects' [MC] (CALL Nov 2024), contracts are fixed-price with no escalation [MC] (CALL Jun 2025), and the customer sets the procurement rules. A moat that guarantees you the work but not the price is worth far less than the scores above imply. [AI]

**Is the moat a company asset or a state asset?** MDL's qualification, its nomination for repeat submarine work, its land, its technology partnerships and its board are all conferred or approved by the same ministry that owns 81.22% of the equity and also owns GRSE, GSL and HSL [F] (AR2026 p.117) (AR2026 p.99). If the state chose to qualify a second submarine yard, or to route the next frigate programme elsewhere as it did the corvette [MC] (CALL Jun 2025), the moat would narrow without MDL doing anything wrong. No disclosure in the documents addresses this dependency. [AI]

blocks.text: MDL's moat is real, narrow and asymmetric: **very strong protection against losing submarine work, very weak protection against earning poor returns on everything else.** The regulatory and switching-cost factors would justify a premium multiple for a business earning a contractual return; the input-control and technology factors say that the return is set by the customer and by input costs that MDL cannot pass through. The correct way to hold both thoughts is that the moat protects the franchise's existence, not its profitability. [AI]

sections.title: Forecast model: interpreting the base case

blocks.text: All projections in this report come from our DCF model and none are our own construction. The method is a five-year free cash flow to firm build: EBITDA less tax on EBIT less capex less the change in net working capital, with sales growth fading linearly from a starting rate to a year-five rate, a Gordon terminal value, and equity value derived as enterprise value less borrowings. [F] (NUMBERS)

columns: Basis as stated in the model

subsections.title: Base-case assumptions and what they embed

items: The base case assumes MDL compounds sales at 18.4% next year, fading to 10% by year five - an average of about 14.2% over five years [F] (NUMBERS). Against the contracted order book of Rs 18,218 cr, that growth cannot be delivered from the current backlog: it requires new awards. [AI] (PPT Jul 2026)

It assumes a 17% EBITDA margin held flat for five years [F] (NUMBERS). Management's own guidance for new projects is 12-15% at PBT level [MC] (CALL Nov 2025), and Q1 FY27 operating margin was 15% [F] (NUMBERS). The base case is therefore at the optimistic end of management's own range. [AI]

It assumes zero working-capital days [F] (NUMBERS). MDL's actual working capital days were minus 187 in FY26, having been minus 426 two years earlier [F] (NUMBERS). A zero-days assumption is conservative relative to history but is the right choice given the customer-advance cushion is demonstrably shrinking. [AI]

It assumes capex of depreciation plus new sales over a 7.8x fixed-asset turnover [F] (NUMBERS). This is materially below the Rs 5,000-18,000 cr greenfield ambition management has described [MC] (CALL Nov 2025), which is appropriate - that capex is not committed. [AI]

The discount rate of 15% with a 1.15 beta and 5.5% terminal growth [F] (NUMBERS) is a market-based rate, not a sovereign-counterparty rate. An argument exists in both directions: MDL's counterparty is the Government of India, which lowers credit risk, but its order flow is administratively determined and highly lumpy, which raises cash-flow risk. [AI]

blocks.text: All figures from our DCF model [F] (NUMBERS). For reference, the bear case produces enterprise value of Rs 12,907 cr and equity value of Rs 12,460 cr; the bull case produces enterprise value of Rs 33,381 cr and equity value of Rs 32,934 cr [F] (NUMBERS).

Qualitative probability weighting, without false precision [AI]: the bear case's assumptions are the ones most consistent with what is currently contracted - 7.4% starting growth and a 13% margin are close to what the existing order book and management's own 12-15% new-project guidance imply [MC] (CALL Nov 2025) (PPT Jul 2026). The base case requires at least one large award inside the next twelve to eighteen months. The bull case requires both submarine programmes plus favourable mix. We would describe the distribution as weighted toward the bear and base cases on present evidence, with the bull case entirely contingent on events outside the company's control. We deliberately do not assign numerical probabilities - the outcome is a small number of binary contract decisions, not a continuous distribution, and averaging binary outcomes produces a number that describes no possible world.

The decisive observation is that **the spread between the three scenarios is far smaller than the gap between all three and the current price.** Bear to bull spans Rs 308.9 to Rs 816.4 per share; the shares trade at Rs 2,236 [F] (NUMBERS). Choosing between the scenarios changes the answer by about Rs 500 per share; the distance from the bull case to the market price is roughly Rs 1,420 per share.

subsections.title: Multiples against the disclosed peer set

blocks.text: **No peer multiple comparison is possible from this evidence set.** The annual report contains no competitor benchmarking, and the earnings calls name GRSE, Goa Shipyard, Hindustan Shipyard, Cochin Shipyard and L&T without any financial data [MC] (CALL Jun 2025) (CALL Nov 2025) (AR2026 p.231). The single quantified peer datapoint is Goa Shipyard, disclosed only because MDL equity-accounts it: FY26 revenue Rs 3,764.30 cr and PBT Rs 442.28 cr, an 11.7% PBT margin [E] (AR2026 p.69) - against MDL's 25% [F] (AR2026 p.39). Goa Shipyard is unlisted, so no multiple exists for it. On the earnings call, the CMD invited investors to look at listed shipyards' margins to gauge the general range and said MDL 'exceeded the general profit margin significantly' [MC] (CALL Jun 2025); we treat that as management context, not as a benchmark.

subsections.title: Interpreting the DCF and its assumptions

items: The model values MDL's equity at Rs 23,054 cr in the base case against a market capitalisation of Rs 90,196 cr [F] (NUMBERS) - the market is paying roughly 3.9x the base-case equity value [E].

The model's implied exit is not aggressive: a 17% margin held flat, 10% terminal-year growth, 5.5% perpetual growth and a 15% WACC [F] (NUMBERS). Against management's own guidance of 12-15% PBT margins for new projects [MC] (CALL Nov 2025), the margin assumption is generous, not conservative.

The model is most vulnerable on the growth path, not on the discount rate. The sensitivity grid moves the answer by at most about Rs 300 per share across a 3-point WACC range and a 2-point terminal growth range [F] (NUMBERS).

The single largest interpretive caveat is the cash treatment described above: the model deducts Rs 447 cr of borrowings and adds no cash [F] (NUMBERS). Even a generous view of MDL's 'own' cash would not bridge the gap to the market price, but it is the honest counter-argument to the bear case and we state it plainly. [AI]

Against reported TTM earnings, the shares trade at 31.6x with TTM PAT of Rs 2,854 cr [F] (NUMBERS) - a multiple that is not extreme in isolation, which is precisely why the DCF and reverse DCF are the more informative lenses here: the earnings being capitalised are 35-40% non-operating and have not converted to cash [E] (NUMBERS) (AR2026 p.209). [AI]

sections.title: What is priced in: the reverse DCF

blocks.caption: Reverse DCF
rows: Implied constant five-year sales CAGR required to justify today's enterprise value
[F] (NUMBERS), at the base margin, the same WACC and the same terminal growth

blocks.text: To justify the current enterprise value on the model's own margin, discount rate and terminal growth, MDL would have to grow sales at about 56% a year for five consecutive years [F] (NUMBERS). That would take revenue from Rs 13,323 cr to roughly Rs 122,000 cr - about nine times the current level [E] (NUMBERS). For context, the entire naval order pipeline management has described across LPD, MCMV, P17B, next-generation destroyers and both submarine programmes sums to roughly Rs 2.0-2.3 lakh crore of **contract value spread over seven to nine years each** [E] (CALL Nov 2025) (CALL Jun 2025). MDL would need to win essentially all of it and recognise it several times faster than any programme in its history.

**The required growth rate is roughly twice MDL's best-ever five-year growth rate (26.3%), roughly double the bull case's starting growth (27.8%), and about four times the base case (14.2%).** [E] (NUMBERS) It is not a rate that any combination of currently identifiable contracts can produce. On the evidence in this file, the share price is not discounting the business; it is discounting a re-rating of Indian defence assets as a class.

A second reading of the same arithmetic reinforces the point. The bull case - both submarine programmes, 19% margins, 27.8% starting growth - produces Rs 816.4 per share, which is 63.5% below the current price [F] (NUMBERS). In other words, **an investor who is right about the most optimistic operating scenario in this model still loses money on these assumptions.** [AI]

In fairness, the reverse DCF is not the last word, and three counter-arguments deserve a hearing. First, the model's equity bridge adds back no cash; MDL held Rs 12,878 cr of standalone cash and bank balances at 31 March 2026 [E] (AR2026 p.167), and even the conservative portion management calls 'our margin' - about Rs 6,000 cr [MC] (CALL Jun 2025) - is a material fraction of the base-case equity value of Rs 23,054 cr [F] (NUMBERS). Second, a 15% WACC embeds a 1.15 beta on a company whose principal counterparty is the sovereign; a lower rate lifts value, though the sensitivity grid shows the effect is bounded at roughly Rs 760 per share even at 13.5% WACC and 6.5% terminal growth [F] (NUMBERS). Third, a DCF built on a 17% margin and fading growth cannot capture option value on a step-change award: a Rs 1 lakh crore order book, if it materialised, would change the shape of the cash flow stream, not just its level [MC] (CALL Nov 2025).

Our assessment of those counter-arguments: they are real and they are not remotely sufficient. Cash, a lower discount rate and the full bull case stacked together still leave the model far below the traded price, and the strategic-asset argument - that a sole-source national submarine yard should not be valued on discounted cash flow at all - is an argument about what MDL is worth to the Republic of India, not about what it is worth to a minority shareholder receiving a 0.81% dividend yield [F] (NUMBERS). [AI]

sections.title: Final thesis

blocks.text: MDL owns something that cannot be bought: state qualification to build conventional submarines and destroyers, two independent submarine assembly and launch lines, a trained integration workforce, and a 65-year relationship with the only customer that matters [F] (AR2026 p.32) (AR2026 p.42). That position was validated in the hardest possible way over FY22-FY26, when the company delivered four destroyers and four frigates, all the destroyers ahead of contractual timeline, while tripling revenue and lifting operating margin from 6% to 17% [F] (AR2026 p.68) (NUMBERS). It carries no debt at the parent, holds Rs 12,878 cr of cash and bank balances, earns a 36% return on capital employed and pays out about 30% of profit [F] (AR2026 p.167) (NUMBERS) (AR2026 p.34). The identified pipeline - P75-AS, P75I, P17B, MCMV, LPD and next-generation destroyers - is larger in aggregate than anything MDL has ever addressed [MC] (CALL Nov 2025), and the indigenisation record gives it a policy tailwind that is real and quantified [F] (AR2026 p.44).

Every one of those strengths is a statement about the asset rather than about the shareholder's claim on it. The order book has fallen 60% in four years to Rs 18,218 cr, of which 52% relates to programmes on which every vessel has already been delivered [F] (AR2026 p.36) (PPT Jul 2026) [E]. The contracts that would refill it have been guided as imminent three times in twelve months and remain unsigned [MC] (CALL Feb 2025) (CALL Jun 2025) (CALL Nov 2025). The work that has replaced them carries a Rs 1,060 cr provision for expected losses [F] (AR2026 p.153). Reported profit has not been cash - operating cash flow is 0.02x profit over three years [F] (NUMBERS) - and 35% of pre-tax profit is interest on a deposit pool that management says is mostly the customer's money and that fell by roughly Rs 3,272 cr in FY26 [F] (NUMBERS) [MC] (CALL Jun 2025) [E] (AR2026 p.167). And the price requires about 56% annual sales growth for five years against a base case of 14.2% [F] (NUMBERS).

That portion generates revenue without employing the yard, and it is finite.

Missed to the downside: **the customer-advance cycle.** Working capital days moved from minus 426 to minus 187 in two years [F] (NUMBERS). Without a new mega-contract the advance cushion continues to deflate, taking other income - 35% of PBT - with it. [AI]

These are not competitive contests. Delay is a timing problem, not an outcome problem - unless the programme itself is restructured.

Missed to the upside: **ship repair.** Revenue nearly doubled to Rs 1,032 cr with almost no working-capital intensity and no backlog dependence [F] (AR2026 p.208). It is the only line in the accounts that behaves like a normal industrial business, and it is capacity-constrained rather than demand-constrained [MC] (CALL Jun 2025).

blocks.text: The shares trade at Rs 2,236, 27% below the 52-week high of Rs 3,061 and 9% above the 52-week low of Rs 2,057 [F] (NUMBERS). Our DCF model produces fair values of Rs 308.9 (bear), Rs 571.5 (base) and Rs 816.4 (bull) per share, and the full sensitivity grid spans Rs 460.4 to Rs 760.3 [F] (NUMBERS). **The market price sits above every cell of that grid and above every scenario, by between 63.5% and 86.2%** [F] (NUMBERS). We issue no rating and no price target; we simply record that on this model, on these inputs, there is no scenario in which the current price is explained by discounted cash flow.

What drives the gap. First, growth: the reverse DCF requires about 56% compound sales growth for five years against 14.2% in the base case [F] (NUMBERS), which is a statement that the market is capitalising the un-awarded pipeline - P75-AS, P75I, P17B, MCMV, LPD - as though it were contracted. Second, margin: the model uses 17% against management's own 12-15% guidance for new projects [F] (NUMBERS) [MC] (CALL Nov 2025), so the model is already generous on this axis. Third, a scarcity premium for a sole-source national defence asset that no cash flow model can capture, reinforced by thematic fund flows - domestic institutional holding rose from 0.39% to 5.02% in under three years, much of it via defence index and sector funds [F] (NUMBERS) (AR2026 p.117). Fourth, a modest genuine understatement in the model's equity bridge, which adds back no cash against Rs 12,878 cr of cash and bank balances [E] (AR2026 p.167) (NUMBERS).

subsections.title: Investment horizon and when to re-review

items: Horizon. This is not a security whose thesis resolves over a quarter. The outcome depends on a small number of binary procurement decisions with multi-year lead times and then multi-year revenue recognition curves; management's own timeline is six to seven years from contract to first submarine delivery [MC] (CALL Feb 2025) (CALL Nov 2025). Any position sizing should assume a three- to five-year resolution and tolerate a revenue trough inside it. [AI]

Re-review trigger 1 - Q2 FY27 results and investor presentation, for the order book at 30 September 2026 and its delivered-versus-undelivered split, and for whether the operating margin holds above the guided 12-15% band. [F] (PPT Jul 2026) (NUMBERS)
Re-review trigger 2 - any exchange announcement of a P75-AS, P75I, P17B, MCMV or LPD award. This single event would change the growth input in every scenario. [F] (ANNOUNCEMENTS)

Re-review trigger 3 - the FY27 half-year cash flow statement, for whether operating cash flow returns to positive and whether unbilled receivables above Rs 1,577 cr continue to build. [F] (AR2026 p.201) (NUMBERS)

Re-review trigger 4 - the FY27 annual report, for the onerous-contract provision balance, the P17A liquidated damages balance, the contract liability and gross customer advances, and whether segment or capacity disclosure improves. [F] (AR2026 p.153) (AR2026 p.231) (AR2026 p.167)

Re-review trigger 5 - resumption of quarterly earnings calls. Three consecutive quarters without a transcript materially degrades the evidence base, and a restored call would allow direct testing of the twenty-five questions above. [AI]
Re-review trigger 6 - Colombo Dockyard's first full financial year under MDL control, for revenue, profitability and any further funding requirement. [F] (AR2026 p.98) [MC] (CALL Nov 2025)

blocks.text: Our research view, stated without a rating: MDL is a genuinely scarce industrial asset with a deteriorating near-term operating setup and a share price that no scenario in our model supports. The analytical work for a prospective owner is not to decide whether the yard is good - it plainly is - but to form a view on two things the company does not control: when the Ministry of Defence signs the next submarine contract, and what margin it allows MDL to earn on it. Until at least the first of those is answered, the gap between the traded price and every modelled fair value is the dominant fact in this security. [AI]

The guidance tracker in the governance part records every explicit management commitment we could identify from the four available transcripts, so that the next review can test delivery against it. The most significant evidence gap to carry forward is the absence of an earnings call transcript for three consecutive quarters. [AI]

Twelve discrepancies are tabulated side by side in the financial forensics section, including three that do not reconcile at all: the Coast Guard contract value, the Denmark MPV contract value, the two import measures, the quarterly-versus-annual profit difference and the greenfield shipyard location

Every valuation figure - scenarios, projections, sensitivity grid, reverse DCF, multiples - comes from our statements data and DCF model. Explicitly reconciled: the reverse DCF requires about 56% growth; the bull case assumes 27.8% fading to 13.0% and still values the shares 63.5% below the market price. The report states plainly that being right about the bull case is not sufficient on these assumptions

Seven bull points and ten bear points are given, and the strongest counter-arguments to the bear case - the un-netted cash, the sovereign counterparty, the nomination status, the ship repair vertical - are stated in the priced_in and final_thesis sections. The report is nevertheless net negative in tone because the evidence is: the order book, the provision, the cash conversion and the reverse DCF all point the same way
No marketing adjectives; management's own language is quoted and attributed rather than adopted

Evidence is thin in five places and the report says so each time: no capacity or utilisation data; no segment reporting; no customer concentration table; no peer financials; and no earnings call transcript for Q3 FY26, Q4 FY26 or Q1 FY27, which leaves the management narrative about ten months old. A prospectus was not available in this evidence set. FY24 and earlier revenue line detail is also unavailable

summary.one_line: Mazagon Dock is a genuinely scarce state-qualified submarine and destroyer builder whose two flagship programmes have just been fully delivered, leaving an order book down 60% in four years with half of it sitting on already-delivered ships, cash conversion at 0.02x profit over three years, and a share price that sits 63-86% above every scenario in our DCF - so the investment question is not the quality of the yard but when the Ministry of Defence signs the next submarine contract and at what margin.
bull_points: Scarce, state-conferred franchise: the only Indian shipyard to have built both destroyers and conventional submarines for the Indian Navy, and the only one with two independent submarine assembly and launch lines; it is nominated rather than bidding for the three additional P75 Scorpenes and was declared the only technically suitable P75I bidder. [F] (AR2026 p.32) (AR2026 p.42) [MC] (CALL Nov 2024) (CALL Feb 2025)

Proven execution at scale: all four P15B destroyers delivered ahead of contractual timeline and all four P17A frigates delivered by 30 April 2026, while revenue tripled from Rs 4,048 cr (FY21) to Rs 13,006 cr (FY26) and operating margin rose from 6% to 17%. [F] (AR2026 p.68) (PPT Jul 2026) (NUMBERS)

Fortress balance sheet: the parent carries no borrowings, the Rs 35 cr cash credit line was unutilised, standalone cash and bank balances were Rs 12,878 cr at 31 March 2026, ROCE was 36%, and goodwill from the overseas acquisition is only Rs 3.34 cr. [F] (AR2026 p.167) (AR2026 p.202) (NUMBERS) (AR2026 p.277) [E]

Real, measurable diversification beginning: ONGC offshore revenue up 61% to Rs 1,628 cr and ship repair up 89% to Rs 1,032 cr in FY26, with non-MoD work now about 22% of the order book. [F] (AR2026 p.208) [E] (PPT Jul 2026)

Quantified indigenisation record and policy tailwind: indigenous content raised from 42% on the P15 Delhi class to 75% on the P17A Nilgiri class, 116 major systems indigenised, 55 of 174 identified submarine items localised, MSME procurement at 33.53% against a 25% mandate. [F] (AR2026 p.44)
bear_points: The order book has fallen from Rs 45,874 cr (FY22) to Rs 20,535 cr (FY26) to Rs 18,218 cr at 30 June 2026, and Rs 9,548 cr - 52% of it - relates to P15B, P17A and P75 Kalvari, programmes on which every contracted vessel has already been delivered; that balance is spares, guarantee and residual obligations, not construction. [F] (AR2026 p.36) (PPT Jul 2026) [E]

The two contracts the growth case depends on remain unsigned. The three additional P75 submarines were guided as near-certain in February 2025, imminent in May 2025, and by October 2025 had become 'we haven't received an update'; P75I was expected within FY26. Neither is in the 30 June 2026 order book and no award appears in exchange filings through 8 September 2026. [MC] (CALL Feb 2025) (CALL Jun 2025) (CALL Nov 2025) [F] (PPT Jul 2026) (ANNOUNCEMENTS)

Accounting profit is not cash: operating cash flow was 0.02x reported profit over three years and minus Rs 2,654 cr in FY26, three-year free cash flow is minus Rs 1,183 cr, and 35% of FY26 pre-tax profit was other income, almost entirely interest on a customer-advance-funded deposit pool that fell by roughly Rs 3,272 cr during the year. [F] (NUMBERS) (AR2026 p.209) [E] (AR2026 p.167)

The replacement order book is already loss-making and management's own normalised margin guidance is far below reported margins: the provision for expected loss on onerous fixed-price contracts doubled from Rs 521 cr to Rs 1,060 cr on the Coast Guard fast patrol vessels and Danish multipurpose vessels and was flagged as a key audit matter, while successive CMDs and CFOs have guided to 12-15% PBT margin against 25% reported in FY26 - and the convergence has started, with operating margin at 14% in Q4 FY26 and 15% in Q1 FY27.
